title: Wanix — Plan 9 Reincarnated for the Age of Agents
persona: all four personas (Maya, Devraj, Theo, Aria)
oneLiner: A Rust-native, Plan 9-style OS core that runs outside Chrome: everything is a file, every process has its own namespace, and one 9P contract reaches local services and remote machines alike.
outline: The 30-second hero: wanix qjs examples/qjs-demo.js -> 'outside Chrome: true'
The one-line thesis and what it means
Four persona on-ramps: 'I want to run JS', 'I want to wire machines together', 'I'm extending the core', 'I want the deep idea'
What Wanix is (and is not): native runtime, browser is a client, not the foundation
Quickstart commands block
Where to go next (Learn / Concepts / Recipes / Find)

oneLiner: A catalog of nine persona-shaped learning flows that thread the canonical concept, device, and recipe pages in order — pick your goal and be carried.

Prerequisite badges and estimated times

title: Everything Is a File
oneLiner: Every capability — storage, tasks, terminals, key/value, agents — is exposed as a FileSystem you read, write, and list, so one file protocol reaches them all.
outline: The one-liner: a task is a process Wanix owns; a namespace is its private file view
Why one trait is the universal currency
Concrete: cat/write/ls a #kv key, a #task, an #agent session
Under the hood: the FileSystem + File traits, NormalizedPath, #-named devices hidden from union listings
Payoff: because every device is a plain FileSystem, it imports across the mesh for free
Status / honest limits: device-aware semantics (read_ready, is_seekable, content_hash) are opt-in, not magic

title: The FileSystem Trait
oneLiner: One Rust trait (open/metadata/read_dir/mutations) is the universal currency of the whole system; implement it and you are a Wanix capability.
outline: The one-liner and the trait shape (open, metadata, read_dir, mutations)
Walk #kv as the canonical minimal FileSystem implementation
parse_path single-segment rule, snapshot-on-open reads, commit-on-close writes
Which methods default to NotSupported (symlink, hard_link, content_hash, confine_to_prefix)
Device-aware hooks: read_ready/write_ready, is_seekable, content_hash, confine_to_prefix
Status / honest limits: this is the template Theo copies; keep modules under 250-350 lines

title: NormalizedPath
oneLiner: Wanix paths are relative, slash-separated, no . or .. components, with '.' as the root — the Go io/fs.ValidPath shape — so paths can never escape upward.
outline: The one-liner and the rule set
Why no '..' is a security property, not a limitation
'.' as the root and how service devices (#name) sit alongside
Under the hood: validation, rejection, and where it is re-applied (capsule materialize, subtree re-rooting)
Status / honest limits: path string rewriting alone does not stop symlink escapes — see confine_to_prefix

title: Per-Process Namespaces
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: Each task carries its own private, rearrangeable view of the filesystem tree; a child clones the parent's view rather than sharing one global root.
outline: The one-liner: Plan 9's deepest idea, not 'everything is a file' for its own sake
A Namespace is itself a FileSystem (BTreeMap of destination -> bind targets)
Per-process: Namespace is Clone, so a child gets a private copy of the parent's binding table
Why this is the real source of isolation and network transparency
Under the hood: where the auto-bound #task view lands in a new task's namespace
Status / honest limits: the 9P session/namespace seam still resolves through one shared P9Server.root in the plain path

title: Namespace Binding (bind / mount)
oneLiner: bind() splices any FileSystem into the namespace at a chosen path with first/replace/last ordering, giving Plan 9 union mounts.
outline: The one-liner and BindPosition::{First, Replace, Last}
Union mounting: multiple targets at one destination
Worked example: binding a host LocalFs, a service device, a remote peer
Under the hood: BindOptions, the binding table structure
Status / honest limits: do not hold a namespace lock while calling into another filesystem

title: Namespace Resolution (longest-prefix, union)
oneLiner: A path resolves against all bindings whose destination is a prefix, most-specific binding first, merging directories into one synthesized view.
outline: The one-liner and longest-destination-first ordering
How open/metadata/mutations iterate candidates and take the first that resolves
How read_dir merges entries across all bindings into one synthesized view
Worked example: a union directory with files from two backing filesystems
Status / honest limits: resolution is per-operation; there is no cached merged tree

title: Service Devices (#name)
oneLiner: Named '#' devices (#task, #term, #kv, #pipe, #plumb, #cas, #agent) are file trees you operate by read/write/ls instead of bespoke APIs.
outline: The one-liner: a device is a FileSystem with a leading # name
The shipped set and the single INSPECTABLE_SERVICE_DEVICES source
The 'what file ops this really is' reveal for the four cockpit demos
Why #-devices are hidden from union directory listings but resolvable from the namespace root
Under the hood: how --wanix-services binds them; how WASI guests reach #name from any cwd
Status / honest limits: served #agent is FakeEngine; #kv is in-memory; exec devices are local-trust
demoRefs: Click through the four cockpit demos

title: Tasks Own Process Identity
oneLiner: Wanix — not the engine — owns task id, parent, kind, cmd/env/cwd, exit status, namespace, and fds; QuickJS/wasm are just engines a task chooses.
outline: The one-liner: Task = Arc<Mutex<TaskState>>, identity independent of any engine
TaskState fields: id, parent, kind, cmd/cmd_argv/env/dir, exit, private Namespace, FdTable
TaskId is NonZeroU64; root tasks start at 1
Why the engine never owns identity (ADR 0001/0002 boundary)
Under the hood: TaskTable registry, driver map, auto-bound #task view
Status / honest limits: snapshots are VM images, not task checkpoints; identity is reattached on restore
demoRefs: Create and control a child task via #task

title: The fd Table
oneLiner: Each task has an fd table reserving 0/1/2 for stdio and allocating dynamic fds from 3, holding shared open-file handles that survive a closing source task.
outline: The one-liner: reserved 0/1/2, dynamic from 3
OpenFile wraps Arc<Mutex<Box<dyn File>>> — an fd bind captures a shared handle
Why a service-file handoff stays usable after the source task closes its fd
Under the hood: dynamic regular-file WASI fds mirrored into the table; directory fds stay WASI-internal
Status / honest limits: fd mirroring is the shared contract, not reimplemented per runtime

title: #task — The Task Device
oneLiner: Allocate, configure, start, and observe processes purely through files: #task/new/<kind>, #task/<id>/{cmd,env,dir,exit,fd/<n>}, and #task/self.
outline: #task/new/<kind> — allocate a task of kind noop/qjs/wasm/auto
#task/<id>/cmd, /env, /dir — file-oriented task control
#task/<id>/ctl — bind commands (bind ... fd/0|1|2), start
#task/<id>/exit — observable exit status
#task/self — every task sees its own view (auto-bound at allocation)
#task/self/fd/<n> — selected dynamic fds visible
The blocking-stream EOF contract reference
Status / honest limits: exec is local-trust only; no signals/process-groups; child launches are synchronous foreground
demoRefs: Create and control a child task via #task

title: Task Drivers
oneLiner: A driver's check() auto-selects a runtime by program suffix (.js->qjs, .wasm->wasm) and start() runs it; runtimes register from above so the task core stays engine-free.
outline: The one-liner: TaskDriver check() and start()
check() auto-selects by program suffix; start() launches
Why wanix-task must not depend on wanix-wasi/qjs/wasm — drivers register from the orchestration layer
Worked example: writing a new driver, reusing task_wasi_config
Under the hood: the driver registry and dispatch
Status / honest limits: drivers are noop/qjs/wasm today; discovery derives the list from the registry

title: The Shared WASI / fd Contract
oneLiner: task_wasi_config builds the live WASI config (namespace, cwd preopen, argv/env, stdio fds) once for both runtimes, mirroring dynamic file fds into the task table.
outline: The one-liner: one builder for both qjs and wasm
What task_wasi_config wires: namespace backs WASI, cwd is the root preopen, argv/env from wanix_task, fds 0/1/2
WasiFdObserver / TaskWasiFdMirror: regular-file fds mirrored, released on guest close
is_rooted_service_path: a guest opens any #name device from the namespace root regardless of cwd
What the two runtimes share (WasiCtx, task_wasi_config) and do NOT share (the linker)
Status / honest limits: qjs keeps its own engine-local host import path; wasm uses wanix-wasi-host
demoRefs: Two WASI tiers on one shared FS

title: Wasmtime as the Execution Substrate
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: Wasmtime hosts guest runtimes but inherits no host filesystem or process semantics by default; Wanix supplies live WASI backed by its own namespaces.
outline: The one-liner: substrate, not the foundation that defines semantics
Why Wasmtime is not allowed to inherit host fs/process semantics (ADR 0001)
Two WASI guests (qjs, compiled wasm), neither a second process model
WASI inverted: an adapter INTO Wanix-owned semantics, not a delegation to the host
Under the hood: the compiled-artifact cache as a trust boundary
Status / honest limits: per-room memory isolation is real; hard CPU/memory limits (epoch/fuel, linear-memory caps) are NOT wired yet

title: Wanix-Backed WASI (not host WASI)
oneLiner: Preview 1 syscalls resolve through Wanix namespaces and WASI fds instead of the host OS; #name device paths resolve from the namespace root regardless of cwd.
outline: The one-liner: Preview 1 backed by Wanix, not the host OS
Root and cwd mapping, service paths, fd ops, rights projection, clocks
resolve_path and is_rooted_service_path
Why this keeps the authority boundary at Wanix
Under the hood: WasiCtx, deliberate unsupported errors for behavior with no Wanix contract
Status / honest limits: command-style subset for wasm (poll_oneoff NOSYS); qjs has richer readiness
demoRefs: Exercise more Wanix-owned WASI filesystem calls

title: Host Files Are Not Ambient Authority
oneLiner: Host directories enter Wanix only through an explicit rooted LocalFs mount with escape checks; there is no ambient host path in the default namespace.
outline: The one-liner gently: the task sees a Wanix path, the host boundary is enforced
Worked example: --mount /tmp/wanix-host=host
How LocalFs roots and protects the host boundary; confine_to_prefix canonicalizes and rejects escapes
Why this matters for agents and untrusted code
Status / honest limits: snapshots do not store ambient host capabilities; mounts are supplied again on resume

title: qjs Task — JavaScript Outside Chrome
oneLiner: QuickJS-NG compiled to a WASI reactor on Wasmtime runs .js as a first-class Wanix task with live namespace, fds, argv/env/cwd, and observable exit.
outline: The one-liner and the founding proof
QuickJsTaskDriver::check claims .js; start reads the script and runs it
Module vs eval (uses_module_syntax), CONSOLE_PRELUDE, scriptArgs/env/cwd
Guest JS uses qjs:std, qjs:os, scriptArgs, stdio, env, service files — no globalThis.Wanix
Under the hood: bounded event-loop work, set_exit, the warm module cache
Status / honest limits: bounded-execution knobs are host policy, not a scheduler/cancellation model
demoRefs: Pass process context into a task

title: Compiled wasm Task Driver
oneLiner: Any wasm32-wasi command module (Rust/C/Zig/Go) runs as a Wanix .wasm task at near-native speed, sharing the same sandbox and VFS as qjs.
outline: The one-liner: the second WASI task runtime
WasmTaskDriver::check matches .wasm; start reads module bytes from the task namespace
WasiRunner::from_bytes_cached, live WasiConfig, _start, proc_exit recovery
Uses the standalone linker wanix-wasi-host (add_to_linker)
Under the hood: shared task_wasi_config path, distinct module cache subdir
Status / honest limits: command-style only — poll_oneoff is NOSYS, no readiness/async I/O

title: Command-Style wasm Linker (poll_oneoff = NOSYS)
oneLiner: wanix-wasi-host is a generic WASI Preview 1 linker for command guests; poll_oneoff returns ERRNO_NOSYS, so there is no readiness polling — qjs keeps its own richer host path.
outline: The one-liner and what 'command-style' means
The registered subset: _start, fd/path I/O, args/env, clock, exit
Why poll_oneoff returns ERRNO_NOSYS
Generic over a WasiHost backing, no engine or task coupling
Under the hood: process.rs proc_exit hook and trap
Status / honest limits: two host paths, not one; only the wasm runner uses this linker

title: Two Tiers, One Substrate
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: Interpreted (qjs) and compiled (wasm) tasks built from one Namespace share a filesystem — a write by one is visible to the other.
outline: The one-liner: choose easy or fast per task, same security story
Same Wasmtime substrate, same shared FS, peer task drivers
The differential proof: a wasm task and a qjs task observe identical filesystem state
Pick the engine in the same secure room (qjs / compiled wasm / VM)
Status / honest limits: real-world workloads beyond fixtures and demos are not demonstrated in-tree
demoRefs: qjs->wasm->qjs duet on one shared FS

title: Compiled-Artifact Cache
oneLiner: sha256-keyed on-disk cache of Wasmtime-serialized modules cuts qjs cold start ~1000x; the cache dir is an fd-verified owner-private trust boundary.
outline: The one-liner and the ~550ms -> ~0.5ms win
Cache key = sha256(wasm-bytes); advisory recompile-on-mismatch
Why the cache dir is a trust boundary (unsafe Module::deserialize == native code loading)
Hardened fd-based verification (Unix): O_NOFOLLOW, fstat owner/mode, openat, renameat
Per-runtime policy: WANIX_QJS_CACHE_DIR vs WANIX_WASM_CACHE_DIR
Status / honest limits: strong verification is Unix-only; non-Unix degrades to 'is a directory'

title: QuickJS Snapshots Are VM Images
oneLiner: Snapshots capture WebAssembly linear memory + pointers, not serialized task state; live Wanix host state (namespace, fds, providers) must be reattached on restore.
outline: The one-liner: VM image, not a task checkpoint
What is captured (linear memory + pointers) and what is not (task id, namespace, fds, cwd, env, mounts)
Restore reattaches host state explicitly; task id changes 1->2
Open dynamic descriptors block snapshot — keeps the boundary explicit
Under the hood: qjs-restore, qjs-snapshot/qjs-resume across CLI invocations
Status / honest limits: snapshots are tied to the exact QuickJS WASM module identity
demoRefs: Snapshot and restore a qjs VM

title: Bounded Execution Policy (not a scheduler)
oneLiner: qjs driver knobs (event-loop wait budget, ready-IO turns, interrupt poll budget, memory limit) bound guest execution but are not a general scheduler, signal system, or cancellation model.
outline: The one-liner and the four knobs
What each knob bounds and why they exist for deterministic demos/tests
Why they are explicitly NOT a scheduler/signal/cancellation/checkpoint format
Under the hood: where the knobs live in the driver/runner
Status / honest limits: hard CPU/memory preemption (Wasmtime epoch/fuel) is not wired yet

title: Guest-JS Guardrails
oneLiner: Guest code uses qjs:std, qjs:os, scriptArgs, stdio, env, and service files — never globalThis.Wanix helpers or a read-only virtual-file bridge.
outline: The one-liner and the allowed surface
Why the globalThis.Wanix bridge is gone
Engine read-only virtual files are fixture support only
Control bytes (0x03/0x04) are terminal input, not task cancellation
Status / honest limits: runtime paths must use live WASI providers

title: #term — The Terminal Device
oneLiner: Plan 9-style terminal service: new allocates a resource exposing id/ctl/data/program/winch; data<->program cross-feed with \n->\r\n, winch broadcasts 'cols rows'.
outline: #term/new — allocate an incrementing resource id
#term/<id>/id — report the resource id
#term/<id>/data — terminal/client side
#term/<id>/program — program/task side (task binds fd 0/1/2 here)
#term/<id>/winch — broadcasts 'columns rows\n'
#term/<id>/ctl — only command is close (resource cleanup, not task signalling)
Queue-aware read readiness
Status / honest limits: ctl supports only close; no signal/process-group; resize wakeups not yet stdin-independent

title: qjs-shell (Shell as a Guest Program)
oneLiner: The bundled interactive shell is JavaScript inside a Wanix task driving #term and #task service files — not a separate process model.
outline: The one-liner: the shell is a guest JS program (examples/qjs-term-shell-demo.js)
Builtins: cd ls cat write mkdir rm rmdir mv cp ln -s readlink stat lstat; env/setenv/unsetenv; ps; pwd id status size echo later exit
Child task launches: #task/new/qjs then cmd/env/dir/ctl bind+start, with < > 2> redirection
Reads #task/self/dir as cwd, opens #term/<id>/winch, registers os.setReadHandler(0, ...)
Served sessions (QjsShellSession) pump ready-IO turns and release the terminal on drop
Status / honest limits: no pipes, no job control, no external-program execution beyond the qjs launcher

title: Raw vs Cooked Input & Control Bytes
oneLiner: In raw mode the guest shell owns echo, backspace, Ctrl-C line cancel and Ctrl-D exit; clients forward 0x03/0x04 as terminal input, never as task cancellation.
outline: The one-liner: raw vs cooked
Raw mode (--raw, WANIX_QJS_SHELL_RAW=1): guest owns echo/editing/Ctrl-C/Ctrl-D
Cooked mode buffers lines
Browser/editor/VM clients forward control bytes as terminal input
Status / honest limits: control bytes are not kernel signals; no task cancellation semantics

title: Resize / winch Lifecycle
oneLiner: Resize travels as 'columns rows\n' through #term/<id>/winch; queued resizes are drained on read-handler turns; sessions release the terminal via ctl close on drop.
outline: The one-liner and the wire form
winch broadcasts to subscribers; the shell drains queued resizes before command dispatch
Sessions release the owned terminal via #term/<id>/ctl close on drop
Discovery advertises resize message forms
Status / honest limits: true resize wakeups independent of stdin handling are a queued follow-up

title: The 9P Contract
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: 9P2000.L (plus Google.1/.2 extensions) is the one wire protocol that lets Linux, v86, editors, browsers, and the mesh browse and mutate any Wanix namespace.
outline: The one-liner: one protocol for every external client and the mesh
The supported op set (version/attach/walk/walkgetattr/lopen/lcreate/read/write/...)
Version negotiation rejects unsupported versions
Tauth is deliberately ENOSYS — identity is a transport property, not in-band
Errors map to Linux errnos; the same server runs over stdio/TCP/WebSocket/serve
Status / honest limits: no in-band auth; the session/namespace seam discards uname/aname in the plain path

title: Protocol vs Server Split
oneLiner: wanix-protocol is dependency-free wire codecs; wanix-9p maps fids to FileSystem objects and Linux errnos — transports are thin adapters over the same server.
outline: The one-liner and the two crates
wanix-protocol: frame split, tag extraction, version negotiation, typed op codecs
wanix-9p: fid->FileSystem mapping, open-file state, errno mapping
Transports preserve binary frame boundaries; diagnostics kept out of binary streams
Why a new transport is a thin adapter, not a fork
Status / honest limits: Rust Wanix does not fake auth/xattr/device semantics beyond the FileSystem contract

title: RemoteFs — the Import Half of 9P
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: A synchronous wanix_fs::FileSystem that speaks 9P to a remote server, so binding it splices a remote namespace (files and #-devices alike) into your own.
outline: The one-liner: the photographic negative of serve_stream
Reuses the existing wanix-protocol codecs (no new wire format), depends only on wanix-fs + wanix-protocol
Concurrency: Arc<Mutex<P9Conn>>, one request outstanding
The five hostile-peer corrections: frame-size ceiling, honest seekability, RAII fid guards, bounded read_dir, server-side O_APPEND
Offers 9P2000.L.Google.2 to collapse walk+stat into one Twalkgetattr
Status / honest limits: read_dir is O(n^2) over WAN, best-effort non-atomic snapshot

title: The Missing Half of 9P
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: Wanix could always export a namespace; the mesh adds the 9P client so it can also import one — bind a remote node at /n/<node> and its files and devices become local.
outline: The one-liner stated as a proof: export vs import
Why everything-is-a-file makes one protocol + one bind buy network transparency across every service at once
The argument: write a 9P client once, every file-shaped service any node exports becomes reachable
For a long time Wanix had only half of 9P
The full Plan 9 cast recreated: factotum->QUIC handshake, venti->#cas, cpu(1)->#cpu, plumber->#plumb
Status / honest limits: the mesh/agent layer has no ADRs yet; contracts are fast-moving

title: Import / Export and /n/
oneLiner: Export served files long ago; RemoteFs is the missing 9P client — bind a peer at /n/<node> and its whole namespace (files and # devices) becomes local.
outline: The one-liner and the two operations
bind(remote, '.', 'n/<node>', ...) mounts a remote namespace
Reading /n/A/#kv/<key> drives a peer's device with one client and zero per-service code
Honest caveat: shipped mount-* binds at /n/remote (single slot); peer-id lives in the ticket
Per-peer /n/<peer-id> mounts are a queued follow-up (the 9P session/namespace seam)
Status / honest limits: blocking streaming opens use StreamingImportFs (one stream per open)
demoRefs: Mount a remote peer and run a #cpu job on it

title: 9P over iroh QUIC under One ALPN
oneLiner: One iroh Endpoint per node carries 9P (ALPN wanix/9p/1) over QUIC bidi streams; the synchronous 9P core runs unchanged behind a held-runtime blocking bridge.
outline: The one-liner and the ALPN
MeshNode binds one Endpoint per node from the persisted secret key
Public (n0 preset) vs bind_local/Minimal (testable/LAN)
Concurrency cap: MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS=512, per-op deadline DEFAULT_OP_DEADLINE=30s, idle read not deadline-bound
The iroh version reality: pinned =1.0.0-rc.1, iroh-blobs 0.102, iroh-gossip 0.100
Status / honest limits: iroh is a release-candidate wave; blob plane upstream-flagged experimental

title: The async/sync Bridge Confined to One Seam
oneLiner: iroh and tokio live only in wanix-mesh; BlockingDuplex drives async QUIC streams on a held runtime Handle (never block_on on a worker), so the whole 9P core stays transport-free.
outline: The one-liner and the single-edge rule
BlockingReader/BlockingWriter/BlockingDuplex on a held runtime Handle
Why never Handle::current().block_on on a worker thread (it panics)
Inbound in spawn_blocking; outbound FileSystem calls on non-runtime threads
Under the hood: duplex.rs is the single seam
Status / honest limits: this is why every other crate stays sync and iroh-free

title: StreamingImportFs — One Stream per Blocking Open
oneLiner: A near-never-EOF read like #agent/<id>/events would freeze the serial connection, so each blocking streaming open dials its own dedicated bidi stream.
outline: The one-liner and the deadlock it avoids
Which opens need it: #agent/<id>/events, #agent/<id>/reply, #plumb/<topic>/recv
Each such open dials its own dedicated bidi stream
Under the hood: streaming.rs
Status / honest limits: this is the mesh analogue of the single-frame serve caveat

title: Five Hostile-Peer Corrections
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: Frame-size ceiling vs OOM, honest seekability vs silent corruption, RAII fid/tag guards vs leaks, bounded read_dir, and server-side append — the difference between a client that demos and one you'd trust.
outline: The one-liner and why a hostile server is the threat model
1. Frame-size ceiling <= negotiated msize before allocating a body
2. Honest seekability: a Tgetattr at open decides regular-file; service streams refuse seek
3. RAII ScratchFid/RemoteFile guards that clunk on every drop path including panic
4. Bounded read_dir cookie loops (max entries, max iterations, bail on non-advancing cookie)
5. O_APPEND delegated to the server, never raced client-side
Status / honest limits: these harden the importer against a hostile peer, not against a hostile transport

title: The Key Is the Address
oneLiner: A node's persisted ed25519 public key is simultaneously its identity and its dialable iroh EndpointId, so 'mount this node' and 'trust this node' are the same bytes.
outline: The one-liner: the same 32 bytes authorize and locate
~/.wanix/node.key (0600, stable across restarts), raw seed
PeerId is the raw 32-byte public key; equality by key; hex is the 64-char display
Public key = identity AND iroh EndpointId (dialable address)
Why this makes /n/<node> workable on the open internet
Status / honest limits: in-band Tauth stays ENOSYS forever; identity is proven by the QUIC handshake
demoRefs: Mount a remote peer and run a #cpu job on it

title: Persisted ed25519 Node Identity
oneLiner: A 32-byte ed25519 seed at ~/.wanix/node.key (0600, stable across restarts) is the node identity; the QUIC handshake authenticates it so in-band Tauth stays ENOSYS.
outline: The one-liner and NodeIdentity::load_or_create
The seed is serialized raw (not via an iroh re-export)
Why the file is 0600 and stable across restarts
The server never trusts a client-claimed uname (reads connection.remote_id()); 0-RTT never used
Status / honest limits: no public multi-user auth; per-principal namespaces unfinished

title: Tauth Is ENOSYS (Identity Is a Transport Property)
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: In-band 9P authentication is deliberately unimplemented; the QUIC handshake authenticates the peer's key in the transport, so factotum becomes a property of the connection.
outline: The one-liner: identity is below 9P, not inside it
Why Plan 9's factotum maps to the QUIC handshake
handle_attach decodes uname/aname but the trust gate is keyed on the verified PeerId
Tauth returns ENOSYS in session.rs
Status / honest limits: over plain stdio/TCP there is no transport identity at all — local-trust only

title: A Capability Is a Bind
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: A grant is not an ACL; it re-roots the peer's namespace at a subpath via SubtreeFs gated by read/write rights, so there is no 'outside' for them to name.
outline: The one-liner: authorization is a re-rooted namespace, not an ACL
A matching Grant::authorize() materializes into a SubtreeFs at the grant prefix with Rights
'They cannot name a path outside it because, in their namespace, there is no outside'
The symlink-escape fix: confine_to_prefix canonicalizes and rejects out-of-prefix targets
Default-deny, keyed by the cryptographically verified key
Status / honest limits: exec/agent devices stay local-trust until public auth lands; single-attach-per-connection
demoRefs: Capability grant enforced over the wire
Capability is a bind, enforced over TCP and QUIC

title: AttachPolicy — the Trust Boundary as One Pure Function
persona: Dr. Aria Vance, the Plan 9 / distributed-systems thinker
oneLiner: evaluate(peer, aname) -> Option<Authorization> is the entire attach gate; None denies, and the boundary lives in one auditable place out of the wire code.
outline: The one-liner and the signature
GrantTablePolicy consults a default-deny GrantTable matched exactly by (peer, aname), no wildcards
Arc<RwLock<Vec<Grant>>> shared across clones so it is live-editable
P9Server::with_policy installs the scoped root at attach or denies with EACCES; with_policy(None) is byte-for-byte the old server
Why one pure function is auditable
